name: Caral–Supe (Norte Chico)
summary: The oldest known civilisation in the Americas. It built platform mounds and sunken plazas on the Peruvian coast from about 3500 BCE, apparently without warfare or pottery.

location.value: The Supe, Pativilca and Fortaleza valleys on the north-central coast of Peru, north of modern Lima.

terrain.value: Short river valleys running from the Andes to the Pacific, irrigable land beside a cold, fish-rich ocean.
terrain.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

climate.value: Desert coast. A 2025 study links the abandonment of Caral to drought around 2200 BCE.
climate.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

resources.value: Rich Pacific fisheries (anchovies, sardines), and irrigated cotton, squash, beans and fruit.
resources.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

disasters.value: Drought, and El Niño floods and earthquakes typical of the region.
disasters.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

population.value: No reliable figure. As many as thirty major population centres are known.
population.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

urbanisation.value: Caral’s Pirámide Mayor (about 160 x 150 m, 18 m high) and many urban sites with platform mounds.

disease.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

migration.value: People relocated rather than collapsed when Caral was abandoned, according to recent research.
migration.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

economicBase.value: Fishing on the coast plus irrigated farming inland, with cotton for fishing nets the key crop.

tradeRoutes.value: Exchange between coastal fishing villages (fish) and inland valleys (cotton, food plants).
tradeRoutes.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

moneyAndTax.value: No coinage. Dried anchovies may have served as a medium of exchange (suggested, not proven).

inequality.value: Elite residences and large public works suggest a leadership class able to organise labour.
inequality.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

governmentType.value: Unknown. A sophisticated, possibly religious, leadership is presumed to have run the large building projects.
governmentType.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

keyRulers.value: No rulers are known by name.
keyRulers.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

succession.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

institutions.value: Large storage areas and planned public buildings suggest central organisation.
institutions.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

stability.value: No fortifications or weapons have been found, so the society seems to have existed without widespread warfare.

eliteConflict.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

armyAndTech.value: No evidence of armies, fortifications or weapons.

territoryChange.value: Influence spread across several valleys, then declined around 1800 BCE.

alliancesRivals.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

inventions.value: Monumental architecture using “shicra” (stone-filled fibre bags), cotton textile technology, and possibly the khipu (knotted cords).

scienceEducation.value: No writing. A knotted-cord record (khipu) may have existed, but this is debated.

openness.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

religion.value: Possibly worship of shared deity symbols, with sunken circular plazas used for ceremonies.
religion.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

languageWriting.value: No known writing. It also lacked ceramics.

artsArchitecture.value: Platform mounds, sunken circular plazas, and 32 flutes made from pelican and condor bones found at Caral.

socialStructure.value: Leaders and labourers; craft and fishing specialists.
socialStructure.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

sharedIdentity.value: Shared ceremonial architecture across the valleys suggests a common culture.
sharedIdentity.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

neighbours.value: Other early Andean communities. Later Andean cultures (Kotosh, Chavín) followed.
neighbours.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

ideasReligions.value: Its building traditions (platform mounds, sunken plazas) carried on in later Andean cultures.
ideasReligions.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

colonisation.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

riseSignals.value: Large building projects from about 3500 BCE, cotton farming linked with coastal fishing.

peakPeriod.value: About 2600–2000 BCE, when Caral’s main pyramids were in use.
peakPeriod.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

declineSignals.value: Drought and climate stress around 2200 BCE; a period of decline by about 1800 BCE.
declineSignals.source: Shady Solís et al., Science 292 (2001); Mann, 1491 (2005)

outcome.value: Gradual decline around 1800 BCE, followed by the Kotosh religious tradition.

sources.value: Archaeology at Caral led by Ruth Shady (radiocarbon dating). Checked against Wikipedia (“Caral–Supe civilization”).

overallCertainty.value: Low to medium. Dates come from radiocarbon dating; the society’s organisation is largely inferred.

knownFor.label: Pirámide Mayor of Caral
knownFor.note: A large platform mound about 18 m high at the centre of Caral.

knownFor.label: Shicra fibre bags
knownFor.note: Stone-filled reed bags used to build mounds, which may have helped them survive earthquakes.

knownFor.label: Cotton fishing nets
knownFor.note: Cotton grown inland was used for nets that caught the coast’s anchovies.

knownFor.label: Bone flutes
knownFor.note: Flutes made from pelican and condor bones found at Caral.
